subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Streetlight Effect
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Streetlight Effect.

hook.text: A man searches for his keys under a streetlight. He lost them in the park—but the light is better here.

buildup.text: The streetlight effect: we look where it's easy to look, not where the answer actually is.

discovery.text: Researchers study what's measurable, not what matters most. Easy data attracts more attention than hard truths.

twist.text: Companies optimize metrics they can track and ignore what they can't. Revenue over culture, clicks over impact.

climax.text: The fix is asking: are we looking here because the answer's here, or because looking here is easy?

punchline.text: Easy to measure doesn't mean important to know.

quiz.question: What is the streetlight effect?
options: Searching where it's easy rather than where the answer is
A type of bias in lighting design

details.summary: The streetlight effect is the tendency to search for answers only where it is easy to look rather than where the answer is likely to be. Like a drunk searching for lost keys under a streetlight because the light is better there, we gravitate toward easily measured or accessible data.
details.whyItMatters: The streetlight effect explains why organizations optimize metrics that are easy to measure rather than things that actually matter.
takeaways: People search where looking is easy, not where answers lie
Easy-to-measure metrics often replace important-but-hard ones
Ask whether you are looking where the answer is or where the light is

faq.question: How does the streetlight effect appear in research?
faq.answer: Researchers may study easily surveyed populations instead of the most relevant ones, or measure readily quantifiable variables while ignoring crucial but hard-to-measure factors. Big data amplifies this: having massive datasets of the wrong information is still the wrong information.

faq.question: How can you counter the streetlight effect?
faq.answer: Start by defining what would truly answer your question, regardless of measurement difficulty. Then figure out how to measure it, even approximately. Accept that important data is often hard to collect. An imperfect measure of the right thing beats a perfect measure of the wrong thing.
